content.thinking:
I notice a timing discrepancy: errors began around 09:33, but P1 reports the flag change event happening later at 09:38:47, while the rollout data shows 40 of 200 evaluations already affected at 09:33 — meaning the flag was partially active before the recorded toggle time. I need to reconcile this inconsistency using the actual record rather than my own assumed figures.

The revert at 09:39:58 is marked withdrawn since the system wasn't confirmed back to baseline yet, and resolution came from a human intervention at 09:40:29 with the flag kept off — so I can't definitively claim the revert itself caused recovery, since the log window for errors only extends to 09:38. I'm now piecing together the causal chain, starting with the spike in account page failures tied to the error rate metrics.

The five-whys traces from the user-facing failure down to a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which only fired once the monthly-spend-feature flag was enabled during a staged rollout — though I don't have evidence for why that code path wasn't caught before the flag went live, so I'm staying cautious there. Root cause looks like the flag exposing an untested divide-by-zero bug, and I'm now drafting contributing factors and action items: fixing the bug with proper tests, adding rollout safeguards tied to error-rate monitoring, and improving alerting speed given the lag between incident onset and the 09:39:17 alert.

I also want to flag a process gap: Argus marked the incident as withdrawn based on a check at 09:40:29 that appeared premature, even though metrics show recovery happened at that same moment — so the verdict and the human resolution landed simultaneously, and I should call this out as a timing/reconciliation issue between flag-change logs and evaluation checks.

For the executive summary and lessons-learned section, I'm being careful to use actual figures and timestamps rather than vague wording, noting what went well (quick candidate identification, fast revert, limited blast radius) versus what went wrong (late alerting, premature withdrawal verdict) before writing the final report.

action_items.item: Fix the division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 and add a test that runs the account page with monthly-spend-feature on, including the zero-value case. Do not re-enable the flag until both are done.
Roll flags out to the account page in stages, and have the flag system turn a flag off automatically if the service error rate rises after it is enabled.
Show recent flag changes next to the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop, and page on a sharp error-rate rise sooner so detection does not wait for the current threshold.
Find out why the flag change event is stamped after the first on-evaluations in the logs. Fix the event timestamp or the rollout path so change records match when a flag took effect.
Make Argus re-check the service after a wait long enough for per-minute metrics to settle before it judges a mitigation, and let a human resolution that follows a revert count toward the verdict.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers loading the account page got errors. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, and the service logged repeated account page warnings over the same minutes.
The failing account page requests raised a ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47.

That code path ran because monthly-spend-feature was evaluated as on. Evaluations from {G971b.1} showed the flag on for part of the traffic, and it was on for every evaluation logged from {Gce95.4}. Before that it was off.
The flag had been switched on by an admin through a flag toggle. The change record is the only production change in the window.
Nothing in the record shows why the division by zero was never caught before the flag went on. The spend summary code was not read during the incident, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-summary code path could be enabled for production traffic with a divide-by-zero bug in it. Nothing shown in the record exercised that path with the flag on before release.
The flag took effect for all account page traffic with no staged rollout and no automatic rollback on error rate, so the failure reached many shoppers and stayed until someone intervened.
The alert was raised {alert_raised - began} after the errors began, and nothing tied the error rise to the flag change until Argus investigated.

The flag change record is stamped {P1.1}, after the onset at {began}, while the flag evaluation logs show the flag on from {G971b.1}. The change record cannot be trusted to date a rollout, which makes cause and timing harder to confirm.

Argus checked the service right after the revert, found it not yet at baseline, and judged the action withdrawn. The metrics recovered at {recovered}, so the verdict did not reflect the outcome and left the revert unconfirmed.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, a share of shoppers who opened their account page got an error. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The cause was a new spend-summary feature, controlled by a feature flag, that was switched on and hit a division-by-zero bug on the account page. Argus linked the errors to the flag and switched it back off. A person then marked the incident resolved and kept the flag off, and the error rate returned to normal at the same moment. Argus's own check ran before the metrics had recovered, so it recorded its revert as withdrawn instead of confirmed. The bug is still in the code and has not been fixed.

got_lucky: The fault sat behind a flag, so turning it off was a quick and safe way to stop the failures.
Latency, CPU and memory stayed flat, so the failure stayed confined to the account page rather than spreading to other pages.
went_well: Argus found the likely cause within seconds of starting, by comparing the change, the flag history and the logs.
The mitigation was a flag revert, which was fast and left the code alone.
The checkout team was told that the flag stays off.
went_wrong: Errors ran from {began} while the alert came only at {alert_raised}.
The verdict on the revert was WITHDRAWN, and the revert was recorded as still in place, even though metrics recovered at {recovered}. The effect of the revert was never confirmed by Argus itself.
The change record and the flag evaluation logs disagree on when the flag was enabled.

input.root_cause: Switching on the feature flag monthly-spend-feature sent account page requests down a code path that divides by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, so every request that evaluated the flag as on failed with a ZeroDivisionError.
